patches.old: When interpreting bar graphs with error bars, overlapping error bars do *not* necessarily mean the difference is statistically non-significant—that determination requires inferential statistics. Conversely, non-overlapping error bars suggest (but do not confirm) statistical significance.
patches.new:
What you may conclude from error bars depends entirely on **which kind of bar is drawn**, and the figure legend is the only place that tells you. The three cases behave differently:

- **SD bars**: overlap or a gap tells you very little. SD describes the scatter of individuals and takes no account of sample size, so two groups can have heavily overlapping SD bars and a highly significant difference, or separated SD bars and no significant difference.
- **SEM bars**: the asymmetry here is the part students get wrong. If SEM bars **overlap** and the two sample sizes are similar, the p value is well above 0.05, so the difference is not significant. The reverse does **not** hold: SEM bars that merely stop short of each other are not yet significant — p reaches about 0.05 only once there is a gap of roughly one SEM between them.
- **95% confidence interval bars**: these are the most generous. Two 95% CI bars can overlap by as much as about half the length of one arm and the difference will still be significant at 0.05; if they only just touch, the difference is already highly significant.

None of this replaces an actual significance test, and a passage that reports a p value has settled the question. But when a figure gives you only bars, knowing which type is plotted turns a vague impression into a usable inference.

sources.title: Cumming, Fidler & Vaux, “Error bars in experimental biology”, J Cell Biol 177(1):7–11 (2007) — p = 0.05 is not reached until SEM bars are separated by about one SEM, while 95% CI bars can overlap by about half an arm and still be significant
GraphPad, “What you can conclude when two error bars overlap (or don't)” — overlapping SEM bars with similar sample sizes imply p well above 0.05, while SD-bar overlap implies nothing either way

visual.title: Shape from three numbers, and what error bars mean
visual.alt: Three plotted distributions — normal, right-skewed and left-skewed — each with dashed lines marking the mode at the peak, the median next, and the mean dragged toward the long tail, with the ordering written beneath; a normal curve marked at one, two and three standard deviations with the 68, 95 and 99.7 per cent figures; and a panel contrasting standard deviation with standard error and giving the separate rules for interpreting SD bars, SEM bars and 95 per cent confidence interval bars.
visual.caption: The mean is always dragged toward the tail, which is why a mean far above a median is the signature of a right skew.
